entries.title: Top Defense Official Purchased Stock in Defense Companies
entries.summary: Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies’ stock purchases came around the time the companies received defense contracts.
entries.content:
Kirsten Davies advises Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on information technology and cybersecurity.

This spring, about six months into her tenure, Davies purchased stock in two companies that her department pays for services and one frequent supplier of defense contractors, according to a financial disclosure document filed with the Office of Government Ethics and reviewed by The Washington Sun.

Davies disclosed that she had purchased between $1,001 and $15,000 worth of stock in Cloudflare and Littelfuse, and between $2,002 and $30,000 in Roper Technologies.

These companies were either awarded defense contracts this year or are regular suppliers to defense companies.

On July 21, Office of Government Ethics official Jocelyn S. Urgese provided unspecified “cautionary guidance” to Davies regarding her Cloudflare, Littelfuse and Roper Technologies investments, according to Davies’ financial disclosure. Ultimately, Urgese concluded that Davies “is in compliance with applicable laws and regulations” concerning public officials’ personal investments.

Federal law and regulations generally prohibit executive branch employees from “participating in an official capacity in particular matters in which [they have] a personal financial interest.” There are exceptions and exemptions, including an exemption for investments of a “de minimis” value of $15,000 or less.

Cloudflare is a technology and cybersecurity company worth more than $100 billion. It was one of several recipients of a defense contract in January 2026 that could be worth up to $151 billion. The dollar amount going to Cloudflare has not yet been specified.

The company is currently pursuing a security certification through the Department of Defense that verifies that Cloudflare’s software meets the department’s security requirements and would make it easier for the company to be awarded future contracts.

Littelfuse has not been awarded any contracts directly from the Department of Defense, but it is a supplier for regular awardees of defense contracts. In 2018, it received a “4-Star Supplier Excellence Award” from Raytheon. Raytheon has been awarded billions of dollars in defense contracts just this year.

The supplier’s other purchasers aren’t public, but the company’s site said it has “a deep understanding of how to meet defense and aerospace needs.”

Littelfuse also acquired a company named Basler Electric in 2025. Basler Electric was awarded a contract worth $40,320 on May 13, 2026, five days before Davies purchased Littelfuse stock.

Davies also purchased stock in Roper Technologies, a software development company with several subsidiaries that are regularly awarded defense contracts. Roper Technologies’s subsidiaries have been awarded hundreds of thousands of dollars in contracts in 2026, along with a multimillion dollar contract for which the exact award amount hasn’t been announced yet, according to a Sun analysis of the U.S. government’s System for Award Management database.

The report also shows that Davies purchased and sold stock in General Electric worth between $1,001 and $15,000. General Electric is a frequent defense contractor and was awarded billions of dollars in defense contracts this decade.

The Defense Department acknowledged a request for comment but did not otherwise respond to questions.

“The more defense tech-specific companies there, so I would have thought that would have raised more of a red flag, and that would have triggered an explicit divestiture recommendation on these transactions,” said Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette, the director of government affairs at the Project On Government Oversight, a government accountability watchdog. “It presents a clear conflict of interest, even if you’re talking about relatively small dollar amounts.”

Davies was sworn in as the Defense Department’s chief information officer in December 2025. Her role is described as “the principal advisor to the Secretary of War on all matters relating to information management, information technology, cybersecurity, and information assurance,” and she “exercises enterprise-wide leadership over the Department’s information technology and cybersecurity strategy, budget, and execution.”

In an ethics agreement Davies signed last year ahead of her confirmation, she pledged to take steps to “avoid any actual or apparent conflict of interest.”

She also affirmed that she would “not participate personally and substantially in any particular matter in which I know that I have a financial interest directly and predictably affected by the matter, or in which I know that a person whose interests are imputed to me has a financial interest directly and predictably affected by the particular matter.”

She also agreed to divest from other frequent defense contract awardees, including Accenture, Boeing and Palantir.

Congress considered a bill last year to prevent members of Congress from buying new individual stocks. The bill passed the House but did not make it out of the Senate.

President Donald Trump has himself been a frequent stock trader while in office, making 751 personal financial trades in September alone, including the stocks of various defense contractors at a time when the United States is at war with Iran.

In August, The Sun reported that Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal purchased SpaceX stock on the day of the company’s initial public offering. The Elon Musk-led company does billions of dollars’ worth of business with the Defense Department and the Army.

entries.title: Wizards Beat the Bulls, 98-94, For Second Win in a Row
entries.summary: Anthony Davis and AJ Dybantsa once again led the way for Washington, who improved to 2-1 in NBA Cup play.
entries.content:
CHICAGO — Anthony Davis had 36 points and 11 rebounds, and the Washington Wizards beat the Chicago Bulls 98-94 in an NBA Cup game on Friday night.

AJ Dybantsa had 20 points, 10 rebounds and six assists for Washington, which posted its second straight win after an eight-game losing streak. Trae Young scored 16 points, and Kyshawn George finished with 11.

The Wizards grabbed control with a 12-0 run in the fourth quarter, highlighted by a reverse jam by Dybantsa in transition. The No. 1 pick in this year’s draft capped the spurt with a layup that made it 89-78 with 7:31 left.

Chicago closed to 96-94 on Nic Claxton’s two free throws with 43 seconds left. Norman Powell had a chance to tie the game in the final seconds, but he missed a floater and Young made two foul shots at the other end.

Powell scored 16 points for Chicago, and Buddy Hield had 15. The Bulls, who lost 124-120 to Washington in their home opener on Oct. 24, led by as many as 15 in the first half.

The Bulls dropped to 1-2 in NBA Cup action. The Wizards are 2-1 with one game left in group play.

Washington opened the third quarter with a 15-2 run, taking a 67-62 lead on Davis’ layup with 5:56 left. Young made a go-ahead 3-pointer during the stretch.

The Wizards carried a 75-69 lead into the final period after outscoring the Bulls 23-9 in the third. The Wizards also controlled the third in the first meeting of the season, outscoring the Bulls 40-20 in the quarter.

Chicago played without rookie Caleb Wilson, who missed his fifth straight game. The 6-foot-10 forward had surgery on his right hand on Nov. 12.

Up Next

Wizards: Host the Orlando Magic on Sunday night.

entries.title: White House Limits Federal Contractors’ Ability to Respond to Democratic-Led Investigations
entries.summary: The new executive order reflects the Trump administration’s bracing for Democrats’ promises to launch sweeping probes.
entries.content:
Under a new executive order, the White House will require federal contractors to notify the executive branch if congressional committees approach them for information about their work with the government.

President Donald Trump signed the order Friday evening, a move that reflects administration officials’ bracing for the potential depth and spread of Democrats’ promised sweeping investigations into the president, his Cabinet and extended circles.

“Certain congressional leaders have threatened to intrude on these executive prerogatives by seeking confidential executive branch information from agencies and harassing private companies that contract with the federal government,” the executive order states.

Democrats, especially those on the House Oversight and Judiciary committees, reiterated their intentions to investigate the Trump administration earlier this week and requested officials save their communications, which may be subpoenaed in future hearings.

The order requires contractors and subcontractors to follow instructions from the executive branch regarding withholding communications the White House and agencies have determined are protected by executive privilege from congressional investigators.

If the contractors fail to coordinate with the administration before responding to requests for information, “The executive branch may be required to intervene or engage in separate litigation to defend its rights,” the order states.

Friday’s order threatened an end to sharing sensitive information with contractors if officials within the executive branch “cannot be assured that those communications will remain confidential.” The administration also signaled it would seek out “alternative means” of completing the work of contractors that don’t comply with the order — including “reducing and even eliminating reliance” on those firms.

“The executive branch must be able to work closely with its employees and contractors on sensitive matters without fear that confidential information will be released to unauthorized third parties,” the executive order states.

Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland) and Robert Garcia (D-California) did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Both lawmakers have vowed to investigate the Trump administration in the incoming Congress in their likely positions chairing House Judiciary and House Oversight, respectively.

On Friday, Raskin warned the Trump administration to save Signal chats, noting that it is illegal to use messaging platforms, including Signal, Discord or Telegram, to erase government records, citing allegations shared with Congress.

The congressman sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche on Thursday pointing to a Signal message thread between an FBI official and an associate of Donald Trump Jr.

Raskin said the Signal chat is “just one of many” examples of deleted communications shared with the Judiciary Committee that raise “significant concerns that DOJ and FBI officials are openly flouting federal law when it comes to the preservation of official government records.”

Also this week, House Democrats warned members of the president’s family, Cabinet and former administration officials to preserve all records and information related to investigations the party intends to launch in January.

entries.title: Trump Says He’ll Work With Democrats to Cap Credit Card Interest Rates
entries.summary: The president made a similar promise on the 2024 campaign trail, but the Republican-controlled Congress did little to fulfill it.
entries.content:
By Ken Sweet

NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn’t deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.

“I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot,” Trump told Fox News Channel's “Saturday in America.”

Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.

Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House’s affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.

The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump’s promise.

That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.

In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: “Let’s cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money.”

Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal.

“Congress should pass my bipartisan bill to cap these rates and deliver relief right away," Hawley said at the time.

Researchers who studied Trump’s campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.

About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.

Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

entries.title: Fifth Circuit Upholds Texas’ Block on Enforcing a Federal Pregnant Workers Law
entries.summary: The lawsuit centers the then-Democratic-led House’s use of proxy voting to pass an appropriations package in 2022 during the pandemic.
entries.content:
A federal appeals court ruled that the House’s passage of a government funding bill by proxy vote in 2022 had violated the Constitution because the chamber did not meet quorum requirements.

On Friday night, the conservative-majority 5th Circuit Court of Appeals found in a 9-8 decision that the House had unconstitutionally passed its appropriations bill four years ago, meaning Texas state officials are not required to implement a provision that provides protections for pregnant workers as outlined in the budget package.

Lawmakers in the Democratic-controlled chamber were allowed to approve their omnibus spending bill in December 2022 through proxy vote because of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic — allowing them to reach quorum and pass the appropriations measure.

Texas state officials sued the Department of Justice and other federal agencies in 2023 to block implementation of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, a measure in the appropriations bill that requires employers to provide “reasonable accommodations” for employees’ limitations due to pregnancy, childbirth or related medical conditions.

In May 2024, the federal government — still led by then-President Joe Biden — appealed a district court’s decision to block enforcement of the PWFA under the same quorum clause reasoning. The appeals court’s Friday decision upheld the previous decision using similar arguments.

The Constitution’s quorum clause indicates that lawmakers “must be present for quorum purposes — as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding,” the court wrote in its ruling.

Judges representing the majority opinion said the rulemaking clause, which allows Congress to determine its own procedural guidelines, does not overrule the need to be physically present for quorum purposes.

U.S. Circuit Judge James Graves, an Obama appointee, said in his dissent that the concern of the judges in the majority with physical presence “shoehorns a much larger requirement” into the Constitution’s existing clause parameters. He also said Texas’ request to avoid enforcing the law was contradictory to the state’s acceptance of the rest of the appropriations package.

“Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause,” Graves wrote.

He added: “Simply put, the majority’s decision is illogical, inexplicable, and invalid.”

The appeals court did not rule on the legality of proxy voting, nor did it invalidate other provisions within the appropriations package, limiting the scope to Texas’ ability to not enforce the PWFA.

Proxy voting has increasingly become a bipartisan issue for lawmakers — particularly after Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida) and Rep. Brittany Pettersen (D-Colorado) introduced a bipartisan discharge petition in spring 2025 aimed at making it easier for new mothers to serve in Congress, though House Speaker Mike Johnson eventually killed the effort.

At a Thursday news conference, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he’d support proxy voting for expectant mothers and new parents once Democrats retake control of the House in January. Pettersen this fall proposed giving members three months to vote by proxy, beginning before childbirth.

Friday’s ruling would likely not affect lawmakers’ recent propositions for proxy voting, as resolutions from members like Pettersen or Luna would not count such votes toward reaching a quorum.

The National Women’s Law Center said Friday’s ruling allows Texas to put pregnant workers in a perilous position.

“Only a few weeks ago voters nationwide sent a clear message that affordability and rising costs were their top priority, but this decision will only serve to increase economic uncertainty for women in Texas,” said Gaylynn Burroughs, the organization’s vice president for education and workplace justice.
